fieldData.name: Urban Water Reuse in Africa: Industrial Offtake, Public Water Priorities and Investment
fieldData.standfirst: African cities can develop an additional water resource by reclaiming wastewater, but a treatment plant alone does not establish a dependable supply or a viable customer contract. Durban's industrial reuse, Windhoek's potable-reclamation controls and Morocco's water-sector programme illuminate different parts of the decision: which water, for which user, under whose responsibility, and with what benefit to the wider system?
fieldData.subtitle: A comparative assessment of Durban, Windhoek and Morocco for utilities, public authorities and infrastructure investors
fieldData.hero-caption: StoneComms conceptual illustration of an urban water-reclamation campus supplying industry; not a depiction of a named facility.
fieldData.hero-alt-text: Water-reclamation basins linked to a factory beside an African coastal city, with a laboratory scientist and utility engineer.
fieldData.article-body:
EXECUTIVE THESIS

  • Reuse investment should begin with a specified water service and a credible customer, rather than a volume of treatment capacity seeking a market.
  • Industrial reuse and potable reclamation have different quality, operating and public-accountability requirements. Their experience is informative without making their models interchangeable.
  • Freshwater substitution becomes a public benefit only when the water actually released, its allocation and the distribution of costs can be demonstrated.

StoneComms original synthesis: The most useful unit of appraisal is the contracted, compliant and delivered cubic metre, considered alongside a separate public-water account. The first tests commercial service; the second tests whether reuse improves resource allocation and sanitation without weakening public obligations. Neither account can stand in for the other.

This is a proposition for project preparation, not a claim that every industrial customer is creditworthy or that reuse always outperforms leakage reduction, demand management or other supply options. The three cases below support specific operating and institutional lessons; they do not establish a continent-wide investment return.

WHY PROJECT PREPARATION MATTERS NOW

On 29 October 2026, the African Development Bank reported the launch of the African Water Facility's 2026-2030 strategy at Cairo Water Week. Its emphasis includes feasibility work, technical design and arrangements that can attract finance. The reported core funding requirement of EUR 75-120 million over five years is a resource requirement, not a commitment already secured. This is a timely context for asking what a prepared reuse project must establish before construction finance is sought. [1]

The World Bank's 2025 reuse report identifies proximity between wastewater sources and users as an important economic advantage, particularly in urban centres and industrial parks. It also stresses planning, pricing, regulation and delivery arrangements. That supports selective investigation of local opportunities; it does not establish that all urban wastewater has a commercially attractive destination. [2]

For a city, an industrial reuse proposal raises several decisions at once. The sewer network must supply a reasonably predictable feedstock. The customer needs a defined quality and delivery schedule. The utility needs operational and financial capacity. The authority must decide what happens to freshwater use, downstream flows and sanitation funding. A credible project makes those responsibilities visible before presenting its capital requirement.

THREE CASES, THREE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS

Durban: industrial demand as the starting point

eThekwini's municipal reuse booklet describes the Durban Water Recycling plant as commissioned in 2001 and reports treatment of 30 megalitres a day for industrial use, including supply to Mondi. This is a municipal description, not an independently verified statement of daily output in November 2026. It nevertheless documents an established industrial-reuse application rather than an unbuilt proposal. [3]

The municipality's account of the project's development is particularly instructive: a nearby industrial customer was identified, technical trials were undertaken, and economic feasibility and guarantees received separate scrutiny. Technical treatment success did not by itself settle commercial feasibility. [4]

The transferable lesson is the sequencing of customer identification, process testing and financial responsibility. A proposed customer should provide a water-use profile, not merely a letter expressing general interest. The relevant questions include seasonal demand, production shutdowns, permitted quality variation and the cost of modifying the customer's own equipment. Durban's history is evidence that industrial reuse can be organised around an actual user. The sources reviewed do not establish a current tariff, return on equity or replicable financial structure for other cities.

Windhoek: control the incoming water as well as the treatment process

Windhoek's operating model addresses a different service: direct potable reclamation. WINGOC describes diversion of industrial and potentially toxic wastewater away from the principal domestic stream, consistent incoming effluent and multiple treatment barriers. These are operator accounts of the control system, rather than an independent health-outcomes evaluation. [5]

The City of Windhoek separately describes industrial-effluent monitoring against treatment-plant parameters, pollution-load billing, investigations of failures and wastewater checks associated with business registration. This shows that municipal oversight extends upstream of the reclamation plant. [6]

For an industrial-reuse proposal elsewhere, the relevant lesson is source control and enforceable responsibility for contamination. It is not that a potable-reclamation process can simply be copied for a factory supply. Nor should industrial-quality reclaimed water be described as drinking water. The user, exposure route and applicable requirements must determine treatment design and monitoring. The institution able to stop unsafe supply is as important to appraisal as the institution able to sell it.

Morocco: reuse within a wider water-allocation programme

The World Bank's Morocco Water Security and Resilience Program, approved in July 2023, combines governance, financial sustainability, water-use efficiency and non-conventional resources. Its USD 350 million financing supports a wider programme, rather than constituting an industrial-reuse fund. Its stated ambition to make 52 million cubic metres of treated wastewater available for reuse is a programme target; the announcement does not establish achievement. [7]

The Bank's current country overview continues to identify wastewater reuse alongside river-basin management, groundwater monitoring and water information systems. This places reuse within a portfolio of water-management measures. It is evidence of programme scope, not plant-level evidence of delivered reuse or a claim that every associated reform has been completed. [8]

The analytical implication is that a reuse scheme should be appraised against its actual alternative and its basin context. A factory's reduced freshwater purchase may release an allocation, change a utility's revenue or alter downstream availability. These effects require an explicit account; a national investment programme cannot resolve them automatically for each site.

A SERVICE AND PUBLIC-WATER APPRAISAL

StoneComms original synthesis: The following paired appraisal translates the case evidence into preparation questions. It is an editorial decision framework, not a validated scoring model, engineering standard or investment recommendation. Confidence is strongest in the distinction between service types and the need for upstream control; financial transferability remains conditional because comparable contracts and operating accounts were not available.

The service account

Begin with the customer specification. Record the intended use, expected consumption profile, acceptance point, quality requirements and response to interruption. Establish which party pays for on-site conversion and whether backup water remains available. Demand expressed as annual volume can conceal a mismatch between continuous treatment and intermittent factory production.

Then reconcile the physical chain: wastewater arriving, water treated, water passing compliance tests, water reaching the customer and water accepted for billing. These quantities need separate meters or a defensible reconciliation. Nameplate treatment capacity should not be used as the revenue volume. Avoid counting a rejected batch as a successful delivery merely because it left the treatment works.

Price the complete service boundary. Include collection or feedstock payments where applicable, treatment, pumping, storage, testing, residuals management, maintenance, replacement, customer connection and backup arrangements. Compare the resulting service with the customer's feasible alternative at equivalent reliability and quality. A low treatment-only cost can conceal expensive conveyance or a cost shifted to the utility.

The public-water account

Identify the freshwater abstraction or purchase expected to fall, the baseline used to demonstrate that reduction and the authority responsible for allocation. Distinguish an accounting reduction from additional dependable supply for households or other users. If the released water is not available when or where public demand occurs, a one-for-one access claim would be misleading.

Record the sanitation service that must continue regardless of the customer's purchases. Identify any public subsidy, guarantee or revenue loss and who bears it. Assess downstream users, environmental flows and residual disposal. Industrial demand can help support a scheme, but should not make essential wastewater treatment contingent on one factory remaining open.

The paired appraisal makes disagreement legible. A technically workable plant may fail the service account because the customer will not accept its interruption profile. A commercially credible contract may fail the public-water account because its subsidy or resource allocation has not been justified. The appropriate response is to revise or pause that project, rather than merge both concerns into an undifferentiated benefit claim.

CONTRACTS THAT RECOGNISE OPERATING REALITY

A long-term purchase undertaking is only as useful as the demand and payment capacity behind it. Preparation should examine customer concentration, production cycles, credit support and the consequences of closure. Any minimum-volume or availability payment needs explicit conditions for water quality and service performance. An unconditional payment obligation cannot repair unreliable supply.

Responsibilities should cover contamination at source, deterioration during conveyance, laboratory verification, off-specification water, maintenance outages and emergency isolation. The customer and utility need an agreed way to establish facts during a dispute. Specify whether a meter measures production, delivered water or accepted water; those are different commercial events.

Energy exposure also belongs in the contract appraisal. Pumping distance and elevation, treatment intensity and interruption arrangements can change the service's economics. This paper does not calculate an energy or emissions advantage: that requires site-level measurement and a defined alternative. Claims that reuse is necessarily cheaper or lower-carbon would exceed the evidence reviewed.

Public procurement, utility delivery and private participation should be compared against the same service requirements. The World Bank's work on water governance treats institutional and delivery choices as part of resource planning, rather than making one procurement form universally preferable. [9] Public finance may be justified for a public benefit, but its purpose and continuing liabilities should remain visible.

PREPARATION PRIORITIES FOR DECISION-MAKERS

For utilities: assemble a shared evidence pack before tender design. It should include incoming-effluent variability, existing treatment performance, customer-use profiles, conveyance requirements, operating-cost boundaries and an allocation baseline. Commission site testing where the public record cannot establish these conditions. A data gap is a preparation task, not a reason to substitute a favourable assumption.

For public authorities: determine the priority of uses, the monitoring and enforcement arrangements, and the treatment obligations that continue if the customer leaves. Publish the rationale for public support and how benefits will be checked. Consultation should include households, downstream users, workers and businesses affected by construction or altered water allocations.

For industrial customers: test compatibility with actual processes and downtime requirements. Clarify responsibility for equipment changes, rejected deliveries and backup supply. A process-water contract should not rely on the ambiguous description 'near-potable' as a substitute for an agreed specification.

For financiers and development partners: fund the preparation needed to distinguish viable service contracts from a general resource opportunity. Require reconciled output and payment evidence, operating contingencies and a public-water baseline. Appraise expansion modules against demonstrated demand rather than assuming that all future treatment output will find a buyer.

This ordering supports a practical first decision: whether to finance the next stage of evidence gathering. It deliberately precedes a decision to finance construction. Where feedstock control, customer commitment or public allocation is unresolved, a smaller preparation assignment can be more defensible than a larger capital proposal.

COMMUNITIES AND THE UN SDGS

The direct website classifications are SDG 6, Clean Water and Sanitation, SDG 9, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, and SDG 12, Responsible Consumption and Production. SDG 6 is primary. The Service and Public-Water Appraisal addresses water quality, sanitation obligations and resource allocation; Contracts That Recognise Operating Reality addresses industrial-service infrastructure; both sections address resource-use accountability. These are thematic relationships, not measured project impacts.

Households may benefit if freshwater is demonstrably released for public supply, but this outcome cannot be inferred from plant capacity. Workers and local businesses may gain more reliable industrial supply, while users downstream of wastewater discharges may face changed flows. Monitoring must establish who gains, who pays and which risks are displaced. Community, customer and worker interviews were not undertaken for this desk study.

SDGs 3, 8 and 11 have conditional links through health protection, industrial continuity and urban services. SDGs 7, 10, 13, 14 and 15 arise principally as trade-offs or verification questions: energy use, cost distribution, climate resilience and receiving environments. These links do not warrant additional direct CMS tags. Goals 1, 2, 4, 5, 16 and 17 receive the lowest treatment in the visual mapping because this paper establishes no separate direct outcome or substantive goal-specific assessment for them. No claim about poverty reduction, gender outcomes or institutional effectiveness follows from their inclusion in the all-goal display.

SDG relevance and relative prominence are StoneComms interpretations of issues and outcomes documented in this research. They are not formal impact measurements, and they do not imply endorsement by the United Nations.

CONCLUSION

Urban reuse should be evaluated as a specified service within a public water system. Durban helps explain the importance of an identifiable industrial user; Windhoek makes upstream control and continuing assurance visible; Morocco places reuse beside resource governance and efficiency. Their differences are part of the evidence, not an obstacle to a single universal model.

The investment question is therefore precise: can a proposed scheme supply accepted water to a credible user at a defensible whole-service cost, while protecting sanitation and demonstrating the public allocation it claims to improve? Answering that question requires contracts, operating evidence and an accountable water balance. It cannot be answered by treatment capacity alone.
fieldData.methodology:
METHODOLOGY

Public-source desk research completed on 12 November 2026. Sources were selected from the African Development Bank, World Bank, eThekwini Municipality, City of Windhoek and WINGOC. The three cases were chosen to illuminate industrial offtake, potable-reclamation controls and programme-level resource governance, respectively; they are not a representative sample of African reuse markets.

The analysis separates dated announcements, institutional descriptions, operator claims and StoneComms interpretation. Quantitative information is reproduced only with its stated scope and status. No cross-country ranking, project valuation, financial model or impact estimate was constructed. The original paired appraisal is derived from the source-user proximity identified in [2], Durban's separate technical and commercial tests in [4], and upstream-control evidence in [5-6], combined with the portfolio perspective in [7-9]. Its application to other cities is a hypothesis for site-level testing.
fieldData.limitations:
LIMITATIONS

Comparable current tariffs, audited operating costs, customer contracts, daily compliance results and independently measured public-water outcomes were not available in the reviewed source set. Municipal and operator webpages can describe institutional arrangements without demonstrating continuous performance. Durban's reported volume is not treated as verified current output; Morocco's programme target is not treated as delivered supply.

No engineering inspection, laboratory assessment, legal review, customer due diligence or stakeholder interview was undertaken. The report does not prescribe water-quality standards or evaluate drinking-water safety. No universal cost, carbon, jobs or household-access benefit is claimed. Site-specific resource rights, permits, procurement requirements and public-health responsibilities require appropriate professional assessment. This research is informational analysis, not investment, engineering or legal advice.
